title: Private Equity and the Future of Law Firms: Investing in AI — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source only introduces growing private equity interest in law firms and a possible connection to AI. It offers no position or evidence on AI-assisted versus automated adjudication, dispute-resolution access, process design, legitimacy, safeguards, or performance, so its relationship to the cluster proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Today we’re going to explore something we’ve both been really fascinated by, which is the increasing interest of private equity in law firms, what it means, and how it connects to AI.But before we dive into all of that, let’s start with our AI Aha!s.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s account of institutional and ownership constraints by presenting private-equity-funded MSOs as a specific mechanism for financing AI investment and scale. It also develops the cluster’s caution that outside capital may create practical control, professional-independence and client-loyalty risks, while treating the model’s benefits as prospective rather than established.
qs: So the private equity firm would provide the cash so that law firms could use the MSO to invest in AI upgrades in exchange for equity in the MSO.
That can erode the loyalty to clients that Rule 5.4 is meant to protect.I think it’s a complicated question.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption is constrained by the traditional law-firm business model and materially develops the cluster’s capital-structure point by proposing private-equity-backed MSOs as a financing route. It also qualifies that proposal with Rule 5.4, control and professional-independence risks, while presenting investor interest rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: If the legal profession is going to be able to invest in AI at scale, it’s going to need capital that the current law firm structure doesn’t allow.

But there’s also been analysis, including from Jordan Furlong, about some of the potential downsides of taking private equity and the risks involved—like clearly defining what you mean by business assets and handing over control of things that were previously under partner control, and the changes that could create.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational capacity rather than access alone and materially extends the cluster by identifying partnership capital constraints and proposing private-equity-funded MSOs as a mechanism for financing AI and shared infrastructure. It also qualifies this proposal with professional-control risks and acknowledges that benefits remain prospective.
qs: If the legal profession is going to be able to invest in AI at scale, it’s going to need capital that the current law firm structure doesn’t allow.
So the private equity firm would provide the cash so that law firms could use the MSO to invest in AI upgrades in exchange for equity in the MSO.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI pressure is principally organisational and business-model-driven, then materially extends the cluster by proposing private-equity-backed MSOs as a mechanism for overcoming partnership capital constraints and funding shared AI infrastructure. It also adds a governance qualification: external capital may create practical control and professional-independence risks.
qs: If at the end of every year a business were to give out all of its profits to the partners, it would have zero for R&D.
So the private equity firm would provide the cash so that law firms could use the MSO to invest in AI upgrades in exchange for equity in the MSO.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s operating-capability and governance argument by detailing an MSO structure that could finance technology and AI infrastructure outside the traditional partnership model. It also strengthens the cluster’s caution that access to outside capital may create practical investor control and threaten professional independence. It does not directly evidence buyer-led workflow disaggregation or pricing reform.
qs: Letting lawyers be lawyers and funders run the tech might be a solution to the way the partnership model gets in the way of scaling.The other side of that, of course, is that when private equity owns the MSO, it’s controlling the firm’s technology, data, brand, and bank accounts.
That can erode the loyalty to clients that Rule 5.4 is meant to protect.I think it’s a complicated question.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s nuanced treatment of transparency by endorsing a judicial order that distinguishes when AI disclosure is and is not required, with disclosure triggered when AI builds or enhances evidence considered by a court or jury. Its parenting discussion is outside the court-AI proposition and does not alter that support.
qs: It was a very thoughtful order about when AI disclosure is required and when it’s not.

I think, for whatever it’s worth, the dividing line for Judge McGee is if AI was used to build or enhance any kind of evidence that the court or a jury is going to be considering, it has to be disclosed.

st.t: Everyday usability: Better formats do not prove accuracy
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s account of slide generation as human-directed assistance: McCormack’s favorable result depended on substantial prior thinking, structured objectives and an existing deck as a style reference. Its evidence is a personal trial and recommendation, not systematic proof of accuracy or comparative performance.
qs: Bridget McCormack: Yeah, I described what the presentation was about, points I wanted to make—and I had actually done a lot of thinking about that.

I literally had, like, three points in three sections and what I was trying to achieve by those points.And then I did give it a deck that I had used in another context, so it saw kind of my style in some of the ways in which I have used decks in the past.

st.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s core position: outside capital and MSOs may fund AI and scale where partnership structures underinvest, but investor interest and formal lawyer ownership do not establish an investable, successful, or professionally independent firm. It presents the financing benefits and practical-control risks as unresolved rather than endorsing MSOs unconditionally.

Letting lawyers be lawyers and funders run the tech might be a solution to the way the partnership model gets in the way of scaling.The other side of that, of course, is that when private equity owns the MSO, it’s controlling the firm’s technology, data, brand, and bank accounts.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition by presenting outside capital through MSOs as a possible response to partnership investment constraints while emphasizing that control over technology, data, branding and finances creates governance and professional-independence risks. It treats MSOs as one qualified organizational alternative, not as proof that capital alone or wholesale incorporation solves adaptation.
qs: I do think it’s hard for law firms with a traditional partner profit-sharing model to build for the future.

Letting lawyers be lawyers and funders run the tech might be a solution to the way the partnership model gets in the way of scaling.The other side of that, of course, is that when private equity owns the MSO, it’s controlling the firm’s technology, data, brand, and bank accounts.

st.an: The source supports practitioner engagement through bounded, supplementary AI use and endorses a nuanced court policy that distinguishes routine assistance from evidentiary uses requiring disclosure. This aligns with experimentation under human control and governance attentive to reliability and judicial legitimacy, though it adds little outcome evidence or broader redesign analysis.

kp.k: Court disclosure distinguishes AI-generated evidence from routine legal tasks
kp.d: McCormack reports that North Carolina trial judge Marty McGee issued an administrative order requiring disclosure when AI builds or enhances evidence considered by a court or jury, but not for routine tasks including calendaring, email, e-discovery and drafting. She praises its nuance and educational resources; the transcript describes rather than reproduces the order.
qs: I think, for whatever it’s worth, the dividing line for Judge McGee is if AI was used to build or enhance any kind of evidence that the court or a jury is going to be considering, it has to be disclosed.
But if it’s used in the kinds of routine tasks that lawyers do—calendaring, email, even e-discovery and drafting—it doesn’t have to be disclosed.

kp.k: AI investment correction need not reverse practical adoption
kp.d: McCormack reports the bubble argument as a mismatch between infrastructure expenditure and AI revenues, but argues against the bear case based on practical coding and legal uses, major investors' balance sheets, and chip and energy constraints. Leonard allows that one or two overextended startups could fail without collapsing the ecosystem. These are early-2026 judgments and analogies, not demonstrated economic findings.
qs: And there’s a mismatch with what we’re seeing in terms of revenue tied directly to AI products.
And within legal, we know that it’s doing significant work here in the beginning of 2026 that is unlikely to backtrack.
We’re still supply-constrained. There’s not enough chips, there’s not enough energy, and that suggests that demand is pretty durable.
I think that there may be one or two big startups that don’t have the revenue streams you’re talking about that could burst because they’re overextended in the commitments they’re making.

kp.k: Recession could accelerate client pressure for business-model change
kp.d: Leonard argues that a relatively healthy economy has allowed clients to give law firms grace despite more than three years since ChatGPT's release. She predicts that a recession could rapidly intensify pressure for AI adoption and business-model change, rather than reduce its urgency.
qs: It’s now been over three years since ChatGPT came out, but there hasn’t been a ton of demand for the business model to change dramatically.
I think that’s primarily because the economy’s been relatively stable and healthy. If there were to be a recession, I think that would change pretty quickly.

kp.k: Legal AI purchasing caution may drive vendor consolidation
kp.d: Leonard estimates that 400-plus AI products are on the market and reports increased subscription caution among clients, contrasting this with purchasing enthusiasm a year earlier. Citing idling pilots, she predicts substantial legal-market consolidation, acquisitions and emerging agreement about worthwhile products during the next year; no systematic market study is supplied.
qs: I think there are 400-plus AI products on the market, and what we’re seeing with a lot of our clients is more wariness around purchasing subscriptions.
Now there are a lot of idling pilots, and firms are more cautious about what they’re signing up for.
I think you’ll see a lot of acquisitions and then some consensus in the marketplace about which ones are worthwhile.

kp.k: MSOs propose separating legal practice from investor-owned business infrastructure
kp.d: Leonard describes a mid-2025 Holland & Knight memo proposing a management services organization structure around Rule 5.4's nonlawyer ownership and fee-sharing restrictions. In her account, lawyers retain ownership of the practice, client retainers and ethical obligations, while a private-equity-owned MSO holds technology, leases, nonlawyer staff, billing software and AI licenses. The practice pays a management fee not tied to firm revenue. This is the proposed structure as reported, not a determination of compliance across jurisdictions.
qs: So how this model would work as a workaround of Rule 5.4 is that the law firm would be split into two separate legal entities.
The law firm itself would be owned completely by lawyers and therefore would be compliant with Rule 5.4.
So this would include the technology, the real estate lease, the non-lawyer staff, the billing software, and the AI licenses.
It would not be tied to the revenue of the firm in any way, because of another prohibition in the rules on splitting fees with non-lawyers.

kp.k: Reported investor approaches signal growing interest, not completed transactions
kp.d: Leonard traces interest from Burford Capital's public summer-2025 interest in US law-firm MSOs to McDermott Will & Emery's fall disclosure of an inbound private-equity call. She distinguishes financing individual lawsuits from owning an interest in firm-wide infrastructure and suggests the prestigious firm's disclosure could normalize such conversations. Both hosts report additional conversations with partners or funders, but identify no completed investment here.
qs: Instead of funding one lawsuit, they would own a piece of the MSO that powers the whole firm.
Burford came out publicly last summer in a piece in the Financial Times saying that they would be really interested in MSOs in the U.S. law firm market.

Then the next chapter of the story came in the fall, when McDermott Will & Emery came out publicly and said that they had taken an inbound call from a private equity interest, in a story that ran in the legal media.
It could be the beginning of normalizing these types of conversations.

kp.k: Partner distributions constrain long-term AI investment, hosts argue
kp.d: Leonard and McCormack argue that the traditional practice of distributing profits to partners leaves insufficient capital for technology and R&D. Leonard presents private-equity funding in exchange for MSO equity as a way to finance AI upgrades; McCormack treats separating legal work from technology funding as a possible lifeline for the partnership model. These are structural arguments, not quantified evidence of firms' investment capacity.
qs: Historically, partners in a partnership model always want to take home all of their profits at the end of the year.
So the private equity firm would provide the cash so that law firms could use the MSO to invest in AI upgrades in exchange for equity in the MSO.
If at the end of every year a business were to give out all of its profits to the partners, it would have zero for R&D.
Letting lawyers be lawyers and funders run the tech might be a solution to the way the partnership model gets in the way of scaling.

kp.k: Shared MSOs could scale infrastructure across multiple firms
kp.d: McCormack proposes that a large MSO could serve multiple law firms, with consolidation generating efficiencies in business operations. She invokes health care, dentistry and veterinary medicine as analogies, explicitly allowing that experience in other industries has been successful or unsuccessful; she does not report measured legal-sector savings.
qs: One idea is that you could build an MSO that supports more than one law firm.
I think that’s the model that has been used, successfully or unsuccessfully, in other industries—health care, dentistry, veterinary medicine.
So the MSOs could be rolled up and grown to bring efficiencies across the business of law.

kp.k: Infrastructure ownership could undermine lawyers' practical independence
kp.d: Leonard reports Jordan Furlong's warnings about defining business assets and surrendering partner control. McCormack reports lawyers' concerns about independent professional judgment and argues that ownership of technology, data, brand and bank accounts could amount to practical control of a firm despite formally separate entities. She identifies potential erosion of client loyalty as the counterweight to investment and scale benefits.
qs: But there’s also been analysis, including from Jordan Furlong, about some of the potential downsides of taking private equity and the risks involved—like clearly defining what you mean by business assets and handing over control of things that were previously under partner control, and the changes that could create.
The other side of that, of course, is that when private equity owns the MSO, it’s controlling the firm’s technology, data, brand, and bank accounts.
It’s hard to say it’s not really controlling the firm, at least in practice.
That can erode the loyalty to clients that Rule 5.4 is meant to protect.

kp.k: Shrinking equity opportunities create uncertain generational investment preferences
kp.d: Leonard links private-equity interest to fewer equity opportunities for ascending talent despite growing firm profits. McCormack asserts that equity partnership increasingly comes through lateral moves, contrasts retirement-focused decision-makers with younger lawyers' long-term investment needs, and speculates that external capital could attract younger partners or repel talent as a sign of decline. She explicitly asks for data on generational differences and leaves likely retention effects unresolved.
qs: So the pie is growing in profits for firms, but there are fewer equity partnerships available.
It feels to me like there could be generational differences in how lawyers think about this issue. I’d be curious if there’s data on that
Most people become equity partners laterally, if at all, and many are non-equity partners.
So is private equity attractive to younger partners because it feels more sustainable, or does it repel talent because it signals decline? I don’t know.

kp.k: Guild restrictions are criticized through historical affordable-service provision
kp.d: McCormack argues that professional restrictions protect high prices and inhibit economies of scale as well as purporting to protect clients. Citing a Yale Law Journal piece by Nora Engstrom and a coauthor she tentatively identifies as a former student, she recounts turn-of-the-twentieth-century auto clubs providing inexpensive membership-based legal services, including complex criminal matters, before bar association litigation ended them. This is a historical argument as relayed by the speaker, not independently documented within the transcript.
qs: Lawyers talk about the guild model protecting clients, but it also protects prices. It keeps prices high and prohibits economies of scale.
Nora Engstrom at Stanford wrote a piece—co-authored with a former student, I think—in the Yale Law Journal about auto clubs at the turn of the twentieth century.
Lawyers at these auto club legal service agencies did everything: felonies, habeas corpus appeals, complicated legal work.
That doesn’t exist anymore because bar associations sued them out of existence.

kp.k: Private equity's access-to-justice benefit remains an open possibility
kp.d: McCormack argues that the current model fails most Americans and urges discussion of business models that make legal information and services broadly available. She distinguishes firms' obligations to existing clients from the profession's wider access responsibilities and raises private equity as a possible, unintended contributor to access to justice, expressly without claiming it will deliver that outcome.
qs: I don’t think the current model is working for most Americans.
Law firms focus on serving their clients, not on serving everyone, and that’s understandable.
Thinking about different business models that could make legal services more democratically available should be a conversation we’re all interested in having.
It would be quite a headline if private equity turned out to be part of the solution to expanding access to justice—a happy accident, perhaps, even if it wasn’t the intended outcome.

kp.k: Personal examples illustrate AI-assisted production and task scaffolding
kp.d: Outside the legal-market discussion, McCormack reports strong slide-deck results from NotebookLM using presentation goals and a previous deck, while Leonard describes Gemini suggesting a narrower quote-selection task and writing template that helped her son complete homework. These anecdotes illustrate perceived production assistance and on-demand coaching rather than measured legal productivity or validated child-development findings; Leonard emphasizes support rather than having AI do the homework.
qs: And then I did give it a deck that I had used in another context, so it saw kind of my style in some of the ways in which I have used decks in the past.
It gave me techniques like: when you next sit with him, go together through the book and pick out three quotes together, then have him pick one of those three.
I don’t want it to solve their homework for them, but I want to use it as a tool as a parent.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bridget McCormack argues that AI is already doing substantial legal work and that its role is unlikely to reverse.
pts.d: McCormack distinguishes the durability of AI use from the possibility of a financial-market correction. Her position is a qualitative assessment and forward-looking expectation, not a measured finding about legal productivity. Jen Leonard similarly argues that AI would continue progressing even if parts of the AI investment market suffered a downturn.

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts that a recession would accelerate client pressure on law firms to adopt AI and change their business models.
pts.d: Leonard says relatively healthy economic conditions have allowed clients to give firms time to adapt, despite rapid AI adoption. She predicts that an economic downturn would reduce that tolerance. Her claim is conditional: a recession would intensify pressure, but the urgency of AI adoption remains even without one.

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts consolidation among legal-AI products during 2026 as firms become more selective buyers.
pts.d: Leonard estimates that there are more than 400 AI products in the market discussed and reports increased subscription caution and stalled pilots among clients. She expects acquisitions and growing market agreement about worthwhile products. This concerns legal-tech vendors and law firms purchasing software, rather than ALSPs delivering legal work.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack argue that AI investment requirements make outside capital increasingly relevant to law firms whose partners distribute profits rather than retain funds for development.
pts.d: Leonard describes a proposed management services organization structure: lawyers retain ownership of the practicing firm, while private equity owns a separate entity holding business assets, including technology and AI licenses. The firm pays a management fee, described as not tied to firm revenue because of fee-sharing restrictions. She presents this as a way to finance AI upgrades while working around Rule 5.4 restrictions. McCormack argues that such capital could help sustain the traditional partnership model. These are the speakers’ structural and financing claims, not a determination that any particular arrangement complies with applicable state rules.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack suggests that shared, consolidated MSOs could create efficiencies and support technology investment across multiple law firms.
pts.d: McCormack proposes that firms could connect to a common business-services organization rather than each operating its own infrastructure. She draws an analogy with MSO structures in health care, dentistry and veterinary medicine, while acknowledging mixed possibilities rather than establishing successful legal-market outcomes. Separating lawyers’ work from technology management is presented as a possible solution to scaling constraints.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack warns that using private-equity-owned infrastructure to fund technological change could transfer practical control of firms and weaken loyalty to clients.
pts.d: McCormack contrasts the financing benefits of MSOs with their potential control over critical assets. She argues that formally preserving lawyer ownership of the practicing entity may not preserve practical independence when outside owners control its technology, data, brand and accounts. This is a stated risk, not a documented outcome from a completed AI-related law-firm investment.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack connect AI financing needs to succession pressures, while leaving private equity’s effect on talent attraction unresolved.
pts.d: Leonard argues that declining interest in and availability of equity stakes make new investment options important alongside AI. McCormack hypothesizes that younger lawyers may favor outside capital to secure firms’ long-term relevance, whereas others may leave or interpret investment as a sign of decline. She explicitly asks for data on generational differences and does not predict a settled direction for retention or recruitment.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack raises the possibility that new business models and outside capital could expand access to legal services through economies of scale.
pts.d: Within the discussion of AI-enabled investment and restructuring, McCormack argues that the existing guild model maintains high prices and inhibits scale. She suggests that private equity might contribute to access to justice, but explicitly treats this as an uncertain possibility rather than a demonstrated or intended outcome. Her historical auto-club example supports the broader argument about organizational form and affordability, not an empirical claim that AI or private equity has already closed the justice gap.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The episode relies on professional observations, reported developments, structural reasoning and historical analogies rather than quantitative studies of AI’s legal-market effects.
pts.d: Leonard supports the consolidation forecast with observations of clients’ purchasing behavior and an unsourced product-count estimate. For the MSO financing discussion, she cites a mid-2025 Holland & Knight memo, reported Burford Capital interest and McDermott Will & Emery’s reported disclosure of an inbound private-equity approach; these establish the reported interest and proposed mechanism, not realized AI returns or completed industry transformation. Both speakers cite conversations with partners or funders. McCormack references experience in other industries and a Yale Law Journal piece by Nora Engstrom and a co-author about historical auto-club legal services. No benchmark results, productivity measurements, investment-return data or generational survey findings are supplied. The recession, independence, talent and access-to-justice claims are principally reasoning or explicitly qualified speculation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion is situated at the beginning of 2026, with near-term consolidation expectations and longer-term questions about firms’ viability.
pts.d: Current AI usefulness is asserted for early 2026. Leonard’s consolidation forecast concerns the following year, understood in this context as 2026. The private-equity narrative traces developments from mid-2025 through autumn 2025, and McCormack expects more discussion throughout 2026. Accelerated client pressure is conditional on recession. Financing benefits depend on adopting an outside-capital/MSO structure; shared infrastructure efficiencies remain proposed. Career sustainability is discussed over ten-, twenty- and thirty-year horizons. No deadline or assured outcome is given for expanded access to justice, practical loss of independence or talent responses.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The projected effects span traditional US partnerships, software vendors, investors, lawyers at different career stages, clients and people lacking legal help.
pts.d: Traditional law firms face AI adoption pressure, investment constraints and possible restructuring; partners may exchange some control of business assets for access to capital. Legal-AI vendors face cautious purchasing and potential acquisition. Private-equity investors could own infrastructure businesses supporting one or many firms. Senior associates and younger partners face uncertainty over future equity opportunities and long-term competitiveness, while retirement-oriented decision-makers are portrayed as having different incentives. Existing clients could press for changed delivery models and face risks to lawyer independence. For the broader public, McCormack identifies the speculative prospect of more affordable legal help, distinct from enterprise clients’ cost savings. Although a prestigious firm is cited as an example of reported investor interest, the speakers do not quantify effects by firm size or practice area.
